4 The Frequentist Paradigm

Inference, the Sample Mean and the t-distribution

  1. 12.

    Under the standard Frequentist paradigm and before the sample data are seen, which of the following quantities are random variables?

    1. (a)

      The population mean.

    2. (b)

      The population size.

    3. (c)

      The sample size, n.

    4. (d)

      The sample mean.

    5. (e)

      The variance of the sample mean.

    6. (f)

      The largest value in the sample.

    7. (g)

      The population variance.

    8. (h)

      The estimated variance of the sample mean.

    Do the answers you have given seem natural to you? Discuss.

    Solution   Only the following three are considered to be random variables:

    • (d)

      The sample mean: X¯

    • (f)

      The largest value in the sample: maxi⁡Xi

    • (h)

      The estimated variance of the sample mean: S2/n

    while the rest are not, with (a), (e) and (g) considered ‘fixed, but unknown’, and (b) and (c) typically considered as just ‘known’.

    • (a)

      The population mean: μ

    • (b)

      The population size: N

    • (c)

      The sample size, n

    • (e)

      The variance of the sample mean: σ2/n

    • (g)

      The population variance: σ2

    Do these answers seem natural? Again, any answer is fine, but some justification would be nice! Under the strict rules of the Frequentist paradigm, then all is as it should be: the only random variables are those linked to the sampling process. One does however sometimes feel uneasy about the slightly artificial distinction between random things (e.g. X¯) and fixed but unknown things (e.g. μ), a distinction which, it could be argued, seems to put the sampling process on something of a pedestal (or is it the other way around?).

  2. 13.

    This question simply tests your ability to use t-tables.

    1. (a)

      A random variable T has a t16 distribution (i.e. a t distribution with 16 degrees of freedom). Find the number c such that P⁢(T>c)=0.025. What would c be if instead T had a standard Normal distribution?

    2. (b)

      A random variable T has a t7 distribution. Find the number c such that P⁢(T≤−c)=0.05. What would c be if instead T had a standard Normal distribution?

    3. (c)

      A random variable T has a t35 distribution. Find approximately the number c such that P⁢(−c<T≤c)=0.95. What would c be if instead T had a standard Normal distribution?

    4. (d)

      A random variable T has a t12 distribution. Roughly, how likely is it to see a value of T at least as large as 1.5? What would your answer be if instead T had a standard Normal distribution?

    5. (e)

      A random variable T has a t12 distribution. Roughly, how likely is it to see a value of T at least as extreme as 1.5 (i.e. no larger than -1.5 or no smaller than +1.5)? What would your answer be if instead T had a standard Normal distribution?

    Solution

    1. (a)

      From t tables, c=2.12 because P⁢(T>2.12)=0.025 for T∼t16. For Z∼N⁢(0,1), P⁢(Z>1.96)=0.025.

    2. (b)

      P⁢(T<−c)=P⁢(T>c) by symmetry. From t tables, c=1.895 because P⁢(T>1.895)=0.05 for T∼t7. For Z∼N⁢(0,1), P⁢(Z>1.645)=0.05.

    3. (c)

      For 35df, interpolate between the tabulated values for 30df and 40df. For P⁢(−c<T≤c)=0.95 we need P⁢(T>c)=0.025. From t tables, c=(2.042+2.021)/2=2.031 approximately, because P⁢(T>2.042)=0.025 for T∼t30 and P⁢(T>2.021)=0.025 for T∼t40. For Z∼N⁢(0,1), P⁢(−1.96<Z≤1.96)=0.05. Note that the Normal distribution gives about the same answer, explaining why we often use the Normal distribution instead of the t distribution when the number of degrees of freedom is more than 30.

    4. (d)

      For T∼t12 we have P⁢(T>1.356)=0.1 and P⁢(T>1.782)=0.05. Hence the probability of seeing a value at least as large as 1.5 is somewhere between 10% and 5%; interpolating, about 8.3%. For Z∼N⁢(0,1) we have P⁢(Z>1.282)=0.1 and P⁢(Z>1.645)=0.05. Hence the probability of seeing a value at least as large as 1.5 is somewhere between 10% and 5%; interpolating, about 7.0%. To obtain an exact answer for the Normal case, we can use Normal tables. The area in the tail to the right of 1.5 under a standard Normal distribution is 1−0.9332=0.0668, or about 6.7%. Notice that large values are a little less likely for Normally distributed data.

    5. (e)

      The answers for this part are as for the last part, except doubled. So the probability of seeing a t12 random value at least as extreme as ±1.5 is somewhere between 20% and 10% or about 16.6%, interpolating. The corresponding Normal probability is (2)⁢(0.0668)=0.1336, or about 13.4%.

  3. 14.

    A dairy claims that the mean amount in their milk containers is 128 ounces. Let X be the number of ounces of milk per container, and assume that X is Normally distributed with standard deviation one ounce.

    1. (a)

      If the claim is true, what percentage of containers will have

      1. i.

        Less than 126 ounces?

      2. ii.

        More than 129 ounces?

      3. iii.

        Between 127.5 and 130.5 ounces?

    2. (b)

      A random sample of 25 containers gave a sample mean of 127.4 ounces. Find P⁢(X¯<127.4), assuming again that the claim is true.

    3. (c)

      Using the answer to the previous part, do you feel that there is evidence that the true mean is less than 128 ounces? If so, why?

    Solution

    1. (a)

      If the claim is true, X∼N⁢(128,1). Under this assumption:

      1. i.

        P⁢(X<126)=P⁢(X−1281<126−1281)=P⁢(Z<−2) where Z∼N⁢(0,1). From Normal tables, this is 1−0.9772=0.0228.

      2. ii.

        P⁢(X>129)=P⁢(X−1281>129−1281)=P⁢(Z>1) where Z∼N⁢(0,1). From Normal tables, this is 1−0.8413=0.1587.

      3. iii.
        P⁢(127.5<X≤130.5) = P⁢(X≤130.5)−P⁢(X≤127.5)
        = P⁢(X−1281≤130.5−1281)−P⁢(X−1281<127.5−1281)
        = P⁢(Z≤2.5)−P⁢(Z≤−0.5)
        = 0.9938−(1−0.6915)=0.6853.
    2. (b)

      If the claim is true, the distribution of the sample mean is X¯∼N⁢(128,1/25). (This would be true approximately by the central limit theorem whatever the original distribution of the data, but in this case is true anyway as the data are Normally distributed.) The standardised version is X¯−1281/25∼N⁢(0,1). Now, using Normal tables,

      P⁢(X¯<127.4)=P⁢(X¯−1281/5<127.4−1281/5)=P⁢(Z<−3)=1−0.9987=0.0013.
    3. (c)

      If all the other assumptions hold true (especially the assumption that μ=128), the observed sample average of x¯=127.4 is very unusual, and an average as small or smaller would be expected to crop up only in about 1.3 random samples per thousand. Many statisticians would take this to cast doubt on the assumption μ=128.

  4. 15.

    [Exam standard] An experimenter wishes to make an inference about the reaction time in seconds for a psychological test which involves a person detecting a hidden image. The experimenter’s budget allows a sample size of n=13.

    Let the random variable X¯ represent the sample mean for n=13, and suppose that the measurements will be drawn independently from a distribution with mean μ and variance σ2.

    1. (a)

      What, approximately, is the distribution of X¯, and why?

    2. (b)

      When is the distribution of X¯ exactly Normal?

    3. (c)

      Before taking any measurements, calculate a value c, using appropriate tables, such that P⁢(−c≤X¯−μ≤c)=0.95 when it is known that σ2=9.

    4. (d)

      We now assume σ2 is unknown and that an experimenter observes some data. The following data are reaction times in seconds for 13 individuals:

      21, 23, 21, 21, 17, 18, 23, 23, 25, 21, 15, 17, 13
      1. i.

        The data are assessed using a Normal quantile plot and it is concluded that the data seem to be reasonably Normal (see the solutions for the quantile plot and further discussion). Is the use of a t distribution justified here?

      2. ii.

        Calculate a value c, using tables, such that P⁢(−c≤X¯−μ≤c)=0.95 given that σ2 is not known, and must be estimated by s2 using the data supplied.

      3. iii.

        Repeat the previous part, but find d such that P⁢(−d≤X¯−μ≤d)=0.50 when σ2 is estimated by s2.

    [Hint: In answering some of these questions, you will need to think about the distribution of the standardised version of X¯−μ.]

    Solution

    Summaries of the data are x¯=19.85, s=3.56, n=13.

    1. (a)

      At least approximately, X¯∼N⁢(μ,σ2/n) by the central limit theorem.

    2. (b)

      When the original measurements were drawn from a Normally distributed population.

    3. (c)

      We know that X¯∼N⁢(μ,σ2/n), so that the standardised version is X¯−μσ/n∼N⁢(0,1). Consequently, from tables

      P⁢(−1.96<X¯−μσ/n≤1.96)=0.95.

      Multiply through to obtain

      P⁢(−1.96⁢σ/n<X¯−μ≤1.96⁢σ/n)=0.95.

      Hence we need c=1.96⁢σ/n. For σ=3,n=13 we obtain c=(1.96)⁢(3)/13=1.63.

    4. (d)
      1. i.

        The Normal quantile plot is shown below: as approximate Normality is concluded, then use of a t distribution when considering the behaviour of the standardised sample mean is indeed justified (this is all that is needed for full marks).

        Aside (not required for full marks): The calculations necessary for the quantile plot are as follows, with n=13. As discussed in lectures, we

        1. A.

          Order the Time data from smallest to largest (second row of the table below).

        2. B.

          then we construct the 13 values k/(n+1) for k=1,…,13 (third row of the table).

        3. C.

          Then we find the quantiles zk which satisfy Φ⁢(zk)=k/(n+1) for k=1,…,13, that is for each k value find a zk that satisfies (up to the accuracy of the normal table):

          P⁢(Z<zk)=k(n+1),with⁢Z∼N⁢(0,1)

          It is best to start at the high values of k e.g. for k=13 we have k/(n+1)=0.93, which (finding 0.93 in the body of the normal table), gives z13=1.48 (see fourth row of table). The left half of the quantiles are just the negative of the right half, so we don’t need to repeat their calculations, leaving only 6 calculations to perform.

        4. D.

          We then plot the quantiles zk on the y-axis and the ordered data on the x-axis.

        An approximately straight line can be drawn through the plotted points, so it looks as though the assumption of Normality is safe. One problem evident is that the data are quite granular, shown by vertical stacking of points in the plot. This is obviously because the reaction times have been measured to the nearest second. There are dangers in analysing continuous data that have been discretised in such a way. (It is interesting to notice that only one of 13 measurements is even. Assuming that odd and even results are equally likely, the probability of obtaining zero or one even measurements by chance alone is, using the binomial distribution with n=13 and p=0.5, about (0.5)13+(13)⁢(0.5)13=0.0017. This is so unlikely as to make us somewhat suspicious of the whole data set. End Aside.

      2. ii.

        Replacing σ by s, the standardised version X¯−μS/n has a t distribution with n−1 degrees of freedom. For n−1=12 we have from t tables that

        P⁢(−2.179<X¯−μS/13≤2.179)=0.95.

        Multiply through to obtain

        P⁢(−2.179⁢S/13<X¯−μ≤2.179⁢S/13)=0.95.

        From the data (in part(d)) we have s=3.56, so that we take c=(2.179)⁢(3.56)/13=2.15. Note that this is larger than the value obtained in part (c) because the t-distribution critical value 2.179 is larger than the Normal distriibution critical value 1.96 for the same level of probability, and because the observed standard deviation s is larger than the supposedly known value of σ.

      3. iii.

        The only number that changes here is the t12 critical value, which must be 0.695 to obtain 50% probability. We then obtain d=(0.695)⁢(3.56)/13=0.69.

Confidence Intervals

  1. 16.

    A candle making process is known to produce candles whose life times have a variance of 0.4 hours. However, the average lifetime is unknown. The lifetimes of a random sample of six candles turned out to be 8.1, 8.7, 9.2, 7.8, 8.4, 9.4 hours respectively.

    1. (a)

      Find a 98% confidence interval for the population mean, if you were told the population is normally distributed.

    2. (b)

      Comment on the accuracy of your answer for part (a) if you were not told the distribution of the population.

    Solution

    1. (a)

      Sample statistics for these data are x¯=8.6 and n=6. As σ is known, and we are told the population is normal, we have that x¯∼N⁢(μ,σ2n). The critical value c giving 1% of the area under a standard Normal curve to its right is approximately c=2.33. Hence a 98% confidence interval for μ is given by x¯±(2.33)⁢σn, that is 8.6±(2.33)⁢(0.46), that is 8.6±0.6, giving the 98% confidence interval [8.0, 9.2].

    2. (b)

      If we are not told that the population is Normal, then we can still apply the Central Limit Theorem and again use x¯∼N⁢(μ,σ2n), however, as n=6 is a little small its accuracy may be questionable (we would prefer n≥10 and indeed n≥20 to be very safe). However, if the population has a not too unusual shape (e.g. if it is unimodal), then this approximation will still be reasonably accurate, and the CI will still be relevant.

  2. 17.

    Obtain a 99% confidence interval for the population mean for the logs of the F3+ data:

    0.79 1.08 1.12 1.25 1.41 1.60 1.64 1.71 1.74
    1.83 1.98 2.07 2.18 2.48 2.74 2.77 2.91 2.92

    You may assume that sample statistics for these data are x¯=1.90 and s=0.66. State what assumptions you make, and how you would go about checking their validity.

    Solution   Sample statistics for these data are x¯=1.90 and s=0.66, with n=18. We assume that the original distribution of the log F3+ data is N⁢(μ,σ2). Hence the distribution of the sample mean is N⁢(μ,σ2n), and X¯−μS/n has a t distribution with 18−1=17 degrees of freedom. The critical value c giving 0.05% probability to the right of c for the t17 distribution is 2.898. Hence a 99% confidence interval for μ is given by 1.90±(2.898)⁢(0.6618), that is 1.90±0.45, or the interval [1.45,2.35]. The assumption that the original population is Normally distributed is crucial: otherwise we cannot use the t distribution, and for such a small sample size we would have to resort to a nonparametric technique. We could draw a Normal quantile plot to assess Normality - if we can draw a more-or-less straight line through the plotted points, it is evidence that the original distribution may be Normal.

  3. 18.

    Find a 75% confidence interval for the population mean for the cuckoo egg length data:

    22.5 20.1 23.3 22.9 23.1 22.0 22.3 23.6 24.7 23.7
    24.0 20.4 21.3 22.0 24.2 21.7 21.0 20.1 21.9 21.9
    21.7 22.6 20.9 21.6 22.2 22.5 22.2 24.3 22.3 22.6
    20.1 22.0 22.8 22.0 22.4 22.3 20.6 22.1 21.9 23.0
    22.0 22.0 22.1 22.0 19.6 22.8 22.0 23.4 23.8 23.3
    22.5 22.3 21.9 22.0 21.7 23.3 22.2 22.3 22.8 22.9
    23.7 22.0 21.9 22.2 24.4 22.7 23.3 24.0 23.6 22.1
    21.8 21.1 23.4 23.8 23.3 24.0 23.5 23.2 24.0 22.4
    23.9 22.0 23.9 20.9 23.8 25.0 24.0 21.7 23.8 22.8
    23.1 23.1 23.5 23.0 23.0 21.8 23.0 23.3 22.4 22.4

    You may assume that sample statistics for these data are x¯=22.57 and s=1.07, with n=100.

    Solution   Sample statistics for these data are x¯=22.57 and s=1.07, with n=100. The sample size is sufficiently large that we can assume that s is a very good estimate for σ, so that approximately, X¯∼N⁢(μ,σ2n) with σ≃s. Hence we can find a confidence interval based on the Normal distribution. The critical value c giving 12.5% of the area under a standard Normal curve to its right is about c=1.15. Hence a 75% confidence interval for μ is given by x¯±(1.15)⁢sn, that is 22.57±(1.15)⁢(1.0710)=22.57±0.12, giving the interval [22.45,22.69].

  4. 19.

    Suppose that last year’s volume of a certain internationally renowned medical journal contains reported results from 200 separate clinical trials. Suppose that in each trial a 95% confidence interval for an unknown parameter (such as a population mean μ for the effect of a drug) was reported. About how many of these confidence intervals would not, in fact, contain the parameter of interest? If X is the random variable representing the total number of confidence intervals which do not contain the parameter of interest, write down the probability distribution for X, together with any necessary assumptions. Write down E⁢[X] and Var⁢[X]. Comment on your results.

    Solution   Considering the confidence intervals as random intervals [L,U] with L and U random variables, we can use the fact that each interval has a 95% probability of successfully covering μ. [Aside]: This is fine, but note that, for an individual, realised confidence interval [l,u], we should not write or think that P⁢[l<μ<u]=0.95 as, in the frequentist paradigm, μ is not random and hence there are no more random variables left in this expression. Instead, as we shall see later in the course, if we promote μ to be random then we find that P⁢[l<μ<u]≠0.95 due both to additional prior information and sometimes to more information from the sample itself [End Aside].

    With this in mind, then we can denote by X the total number of confidence intervals which do not contain the population parameter. If we now assume that the 200 clinical trials in the question are independent, then X is binomial, X∼B⁢i⁢n⁢(200,0.05), with E⁢[X]=n⁢p=(200)⁢(0.05)=10 and Var⁢[X]=n⁢p⁢(1−p)=(200)⁢(0.05)⁢(0.95)=9.5≈32. Therefore, using the plus or minus 2 standard deviations rule of thumb, we should be fairly sure of seeing around 10±(2)⁢(3)=(4⁢ to ⁢  16) confidence intervals which do not contain the population parameter. This could amount to 4 to 16 wrong conclusions being drawn. In fact the situation is often worse than this, as we have assumed the process used to construct the Confidence Intervals is flawless. In reality the trials may not be perfect, results may be cherry-picked resulting in what is known as publication bias, and various other errors can creep in. Medical Science is currently undergoing something of a self-examination, as many experiments have been found to be hard to repeat, partially due to poor uses of statistics.

  5. 20.

    The following data are measurements of fasting blood glucose levels in 17 Type I diabetics:

    4.2 4.9 5.2 5.3 6.7 7.5 8.1 9.5 10.3
    12.2 12.5 13.3 15.1 15.3 16.1 19.0 19.5

    The measurements have sum 184.7 and sum of squares 2404.41. Use the t distribution to calculate a 95% confidence interval for the mean of the population from which the measurements are taken. State any assumptions necessary in doing so.

    Solution   To calculate the confidence interval, the sample mean is x¯=10.86 and the sample standard deviation is s=4.99. To give a 95% confidence interval using the tn−1=t16 distribution, we need a critical value of 2.12. (This gives a probability of 2.5% in each tail.) The confidence interval is thus

    x¯±(2.12)⁢sn=10.86±(2.12)⁢(4.99)/17=10.86±2.57=(8.29,13.43).

    In this example we are suspicious that the original data are not Normally distributed, and this weakens our confidence in the use of the t distribution. Also, we should ask how the data arose - are they genuinely a random sample, for example?

  6. 21.

    Draw a boxplot and, by its side, a Normal quantile plot of the measurements for the previous question. Use your plots to assess the distribution of the measurements.

    Solution   To draw the boxplot, we need to calculate the median, etc. The median is 10.3, the lower and upper quartiles are 6.7 and 15.1 respectively [or 6.0 and 15.2, depending on which method you used; both are OK]. The interquartile range is thus 8.4 [or 9.2]. The lower and upper whiskers can extend down to 6.7−(1.5)⁢(8.4)=−5.9 [or 6.0−(1.5)⁢(9.2)=−7.8] and up to 15.1+(1.5)⁢(8.4)=27.7 [or 15.2+(1.5)⁢(9.2)=29.0]. Consequently there are no outliers.

    To draw the quantile plot, we need to calculate the quantiles. We rank the data from 1 to 17. Corresponding to the ranked data are the quantiles calculated as follows. Finally, the quantiles are plotted against the original data.

    Data i i/(n+1) Quantile
    4.2 1 0.06 -1.59
    4.9 2 0.11 -1.22
    5.2 3 0.17 -0.97
    5.3 4 0.22 -0.76
    6.7 5 0.28 -0.59
    7.5 6 0.33 -0.43
    8.1 7 0.39 -0.28
    9.5 8 0.44 -0.14
    10.3 9 0.50 0.00
    12.2 10 0.56 0.14
    12.5 11 0.61 0.28
    13.3 12 0.67 0.43
    15.1 13 0.72 0.59
    15.3 14 0.78 0.76
    16.1 15 0.83 0.97
    19.0 16 0.89 1.22
    19.5 17 0.94 1.59

    Although there are no clear outliers, the plots show some evidence of non-Normality both at the lower and upper ends of the distribution, and there is a longish tail to the right.

  7. 22.

    A random sample of 100 packs of apples with a professed weight of 1kg were found to have mean 1020g and standard deviation 12g.

    1. (a)

      Find a 95% confidence interval for the mean weight of all such packs of apples.

    2. (b)

      Does the interval include 1kg? Can you think of a reason (which any retailer would be able to tell you) why you might expect the interval not to include 1kg?

    3. (c)

      What confidence level would have resulted in the interval just about including 1kg?

    Solution

    1. (a)

      Answer is 1020±(1.96)⁢(12)100 which is 1020±2.35=(1017.65,1022.35).

    2. (b)

      No, it doesn’t. In order to ensure that the customer can’t accuse the shop of cheating, customers are routinely given a bit more than is claimed on the bag. UK and European weights and measures laws for packets of biscuits and the like are founded on the notion of the nominal weight being at the lower end of a given confidence interval.

    3. (c)

      z∗ would have to be about 16.6. The corresponding confidence level is so close to 100% as to be immeasurable.

  8. 23.

    [Exam standard] [Hint: to answer this question, you will need to remember that P⁢(a⁢X+b>c)=P⁢(X>(c−b)/a) for any constants a,b,c≠0.] One measurement of the wealth of a community is mean disposable income. Crudely, suppose that a person’s disposable income is defined to be gross income, less 25% income tax, then minus a further £3000 to cover some essentials. Suppose now that a random sample of 400 people is taken and their gross incomes measured, with the intention of estimating μ, the average disposable income in the overall population. You may assume that previous studies have shown that the population standard deviation σ for gross income is about £8000.

    1. (a)

      Stating any assumptions that you make, find the probability that the gross income of one person selected at random exceeds £30000 if truly (i) μ=£⁢18000, (ii) μ=£⁢20000.

    2. (b)

      Stating any assumptions that you make, find the probability that the disposable income of one person selected at random exceeds £1000 if truly (i) μ=£⁢18000, (ii) μ=£⁢20000.

    3. (c)

      Suppose that the average gross income of 400 persons selected at random is £20000. Find a 95% confidence interval for μ.

    4. (d)

      Suppose that we repeated the entire process 1000 times, calculating a confidence interval each time (notice that this means taking 1000 random samples of size 400 in 1000 separate experiments). Roughly how many of the confidence intervals for μ that we calculate will not, in fact, contain μ?

    5. (e)

      For the remaining parts of this question, answer without making further calculations.

      1. i.

        If σ=£⁢8000 understates the actual value of the population standard deviation, how reliable is the confidence interval calculated above?

      2. ii.

        What happens to the confidence interval calculated above if instead we had taken a sample of size of n=100?

      3. iii.

        What happens to the confidence interval calculated above if instead we had taken a sample of size of n=1600?

      4. iv.

        Consider the shape of the distribution of income in a population such as in the UK. In this context, discuss briefly the effect of distribution shape on the main measures of central location and spread.

    Solution   In answering these questions, let G be the random variable representing gross income. Let D be the random variable representing disposable income. The two are related by D=0.75⁢G−3000 (or G=43⁢D+4000).

    We know that E⁢(D)=μ. From rules for expectations, we find E⁢(G)=E⁢(43⁢D+4000)=43⁢μ+4000.

    We know that S⁢D⁢(G)=8000,V⁢a⁢r⁢(G)=64000000. Thus, from rules for variances, we find

    V⁢a⁢r⁢(D)=V⁢a⁢r⁢(0.75⁢G−3000)=V⁢a⁢r⁢(0.75⁢G)=(0.75)2⁢V⁢a⁢r⁢(G).

    Thus S⁢D⁢(D)=(0.75)⁢S⁢D⁢(G)=(0.75)⁢(8000)=6000.

    We will assume that gross income is Normally distributed. This isn’t very realistic as the actual distribution is skewed to the right, but it does make life simpler! As D is a simple linear transformation of G, it follows that D must also have a Normal distribution. (If you decided to assume that D has a Normal distribution, then it follows that G has a Normal distribution. Either assumption leads to the other.)

    In summary, throughout we assume that G∼N⁢(43⁢μ+4000,80002) and that D∼N⁢(μ,60002). For a sample of size 400, the averages are distributed G¯∼N⁢(43⁢μ+4000,4002) and D¯∼N⁢(μ,3002).

    1. (a)
      1. i.

        If μ=18000, G∼N⁢(28000,80002).

        P⁢(G>30000) = P⁢(G−280008000>0.25)
        = P⁢(Z>0.25)
        = 1−Φ⁢(0.25)=1−0.5987=0.4013.
      2. ii.

        If μ=20000, G∼N⁢(30666.67,80002).

        P⁢(G>30000) = P⁢(G−30666.678000>−0.08)
        = P⁢(Z>−0.08)
        = 1−Φ⁢(−0.08)=Φ⁢(0.08)=0.5319.
    2. (b)
      1. i.

        If μ=18000, D∼N⁢(18000,60002).

        P⁢(D>1000) = P⁢(D−180006000>−2.83)
        = P⁢(Z>−2.83)
        = 1−Φ⁢(−2.83)=Φ⁢(2.83)=0.9977.
      2. ii.

        If μ=20000, D∼N⁢(20000,60002).

        P⁢(D>1000) = P⁢(D−200006000>−3.17)
        = P⁢(Z>−3.17)
        = 1−Φ⁢(−3.17)=Φ⁢(3.17)=0.9992.
    3. (c)

      A 95% CI for μ would be given by D¯±(1.96)⁢σn, that is D¯±(1.96)⁢(300). If we observe an average gross income of 20000, the average disposable income must be 12000, and so the 95% CI is 12000±588=(11412,12588).

    4. (d)

      We expect a 95% confidence interval to contain μ about 95% of the time in a large number of experiments where each time we repeat the methodology to obtain a 95% CI. Thus, in 1000 independent experiments, about 50 of the 95% confidence intervals won’t contain μ.

    5. (e)
      1. i.

        If the true value of σ is larger than we thought, the CI calculated will be too narrow for the given level of confidence.

      2. ii.

        For a smaller sample of measurements, the standard deviation of the sample mean increases in proportion to 1/n. This would lead to a wider confidence interval being calculated.

      3. iii.

        For a larger sample of measurements, the standard deviation of the sample mean decreases in proportion to 1/n. This would lead to a narrower confidence interval being calculated.

      4. iv.

        The mean and standard deviation will both be sensitive to the very large values of income in the extreme right-hand tail of the distribution, and the mean income in particular will be rather larger than the median income. Most people think a “typical” person is “average” when, in fact, they really mean “median”. For example, this helps to explain the confusion that occurs when a piece of news reports that the national average wage is such and such. The national average wage is in fact rather more than the wage earned by a “typical” or “median” person. Notice how easy it is for Governments and so forth to mislead when reporting statistical “truths”. For example, they might use either the mean wage or the median wage to measure the standard of living; what effect would the large wage increases for executives for the newly privatised industries have on the measured standard of living in each case?

Hypothesis Testing

  1. 24.

    See Assignment 5 - Summative Peer Assessment.

    Solution   See Assignment 5 - Summative Peer Assessment.

  2. 25.

    See Assignment 5 - Summative Peer Assessment.

    Solution   See Assignment 5 - Summative Peer Assessment.

  3. 26.

    Consider the cuckoo egg length data given in lectures. Summary statistics are x¯=22.57, n=100, and s=1.07.

    1. (a)

      Carry out a test of the hypothesis that the underlying population mean for cuckoo egg length is μ=22.4 versus the hypothesis that μ≠22.4. Test the hypothesis at the 20% and 10% levels of significance using the Confidence Interval approach.

    2. (b)

      What is the corresponding p-value for the hypothesis test?

    Solution

    1. (a)

      We test (two-sided)

      H0:

      μ=22.4

      Ha:

      μ≠22.4.

      We know that x¯=22.57, n=100, and s=1.07. σ is unknown but n is large. Thus we can construct a CI based on the Normal distribution. For a two-sided test, a 20% level of significance corresponds to an 80% CI, with 10% in each tail. A 10% level of significance corresponds to a 90% CI, with 5% in each tail.

      An 80% CI is given by

      22.57±(1.282)⁢(1.07)/100=22.57±0.14=[22.43,22.71].

      The interval does not contain the hypothetical value μ=22.4. Consequently we reject H0 at the 20% level of significance.

      A 90% CI is given by

      22.57±(1.645)⁢(1.07)/100=22.57±0.18=[22.39,22.75].

      The interval does contain the hypothetical value μ=22.4, so we fail to reject the null hypothesis at the 10% level of significance.

    2. (b)

      To find the p-value we must find the probability of observing a value of X¯ that is at least as extreme as the observed value, assuming H0 to be true. The observed value is 22.57 (i.e. 22.40+0.17). Thus, values of 22.57 and greater are extreme on one side, and values of 22.23 (i.e. 22.40-0.17) or smaller are extreme on the other side. Now,

      P⁢(X¯>22.57) = P⁢(X¯−22.4(1.07)/100>22.57−22.4(1.07)/100)
      = P⁢(Z>1.59)
      = 1−P⁢(Z≤1.59)
      = 1−0.9441
      = 0.0559.

      where Z∼N⁢(0,1) is standard Normal. Similarly,

      P⁢(X¯<22.23) = P⁢(Z<−1.59)=0.0559,

      by symmetry. Hence the probability of seeing at least as extreme a value is (2)⁢(0.0559)=0.1118, so the p-value is 0.1118 or 11.18%. Notice that this implies that a (100-11.18)%=88.82% confidence interval for μ would just include at one end the hypothesized value. That is, an 88.82% CI is given by

      22.57±(1.59)⁢(1.07)/100=22.57±0.17=[22.40,22.74],

      where the hypothetical value 22.4 is at the lower end of the interval. Thus, you can think of the p-value in relation to stretching or shrinking the confidence interval until it just includes the hypothesized value.

  4. 27.

    The level of calcium in the blood in healthy young European adults varies with mean about 9.5 mg/dl and standard deviation about 0.4. A clinic in rural Guatemala measures the blood calcium level of 180 healthy pregnant women at their first visit for prenatal care. The mean is x¯=9.57. We want to know if this suggests that healthy pregnant Guatemalans have a mean calcium level which differs from 9.5.

    1. (a)

      State H0 and Ha.

    2. (b)

      Carry out a 1% significance test of the hypothesis. Report whether or not the null hypothesis is rejected at this level. Consider any assumptions that are being made.

    3. (c)

      What does your answer say about mean calcium levels in healthy Europeans and pregnant Guatemalans?

    Solution

    1. (a)

      The null hypothesis is that healthy pregnant Guatemalans have the same calcium level distribution and in particular the same mean calcium level μ as healthy young European adults. The alternative is that they differ. Hence we summarise the hypotheses as

      H0:

      μ=9.50

      Ha:

      μ≠9.50

    2. (b)

      By the confidence interval method, a 99% CI for μ is given by

      x¯±σn⁢(z∗)=9.57±0.4180⁢(2.58)=9.57±0.077=[9.493,9.647],

      where 2.58 is the critical value from Normal tables which gives a probability of 0.005 in each tail, and thus 0.99 in the centre. We take σ=0.4 from the European population, since the null hypothesis is of no difference between the populations. The 99% confidence interval contains the hypothetical value of μ, so we fail to reject the null hypothesis at the 1% level of significance: there is no significant difference between levels of calcium in healthy European adults and healthy pregnant Guatemalans.

      Note that an important assumption that is being made here is that σ=0.4 is assumed to be the known value for healthy pregnant Guatemalans based on the value for European healthy young adults.

    3. (c)

      It says that there is not sufficient evidence at the 1% level to conclude that the mean calcium level in healthy pregnant Guatemalans differs from 9.5⁢m⁢g/d⁢l.

  5. 28.

    Poisoning by the pesticide DDT causes tremors and convulsions. In a study of DDT poisoning (D.L. Shankland, Involvement of spinal cord and peripheral nerves in DDT-poisoning syndrome in albino rats, Toxicology and Applied Pharmacology, 6 (1964), pp.97–213), researchers fed several rats a measured amount of DDT. They then measured electrical characteristics of the rats’ nervous systems that might explain how DDT poisoning causes tremors. One important variable was the “absolutely refractory period”, the time required for a nerve to recover after a stimulus; variation of the absolutely refractory period is known to follow a normal distribution. Measurements on four rats gave the data below (in milliseconds).

    1.6 1.7 1.9 1.8
    1. (a)

      Find the average “absolutely refractory period” for the four rats and the standard deviation.

    2. (b)

      Find a 90% confidence interval for the mean “absolutely refractory period” in all rats of this strain when subjected to the same treatment. One researcher believes that this mean should be 1.95: does the evidence support her view?

    Solution

    1. (a)

      The average of the four values is x¯=1.75 and the standard deviation is s=0.129.

    2. (b)

      The confidence interval is x¯±t⋆⁢s/n. To find t⋆, look for a tail probability of 0.05 and 4−1=3 degrees of freedom. From tables, we see that t⋆=2.353. Hence the confidence interval is

      1.75±2.353×0.1294=1.75±0.15=[1.60,1.90]

      Taking the researcher’s view as the null hypothesis, we have:

      H0:

      μ=1.95

      Ha:

      μ≠1.95

      The 90% confidence interval does not contain the hypothesized value of μ=1.95. Therefore the null hypothesis is rejected. The data do not support the hypothesis.

  6. 29.

    Historically, the mean yield of corn in the United States is about 120 bushels per acre. A survey of 50 farmers this year gives a sample mean yield of x¯=123.6 bushels per acre. We want to know if this is strong evidence that the national mean yield this year is not 120 bushels per acre.

    Assume that the farmers surveyed were a random samples from the population of all commercial corn growers and that the standard deviation of yield in this population is σ=10 bushels per acre.

    1. (a)

      Find the p-value for the test of the hypotheses H0:μ=120 and Ha:μ≠120.

    2. (b)

      Does that suggest that the population mean is not 120 bushels per acre?

    3. (c)

      Does your answer depend on any particular shape for the population distribution?

    Solution

    1. (a)

      The test statistic is

      X¯−120σ/nwhose observed value is123.6−12010/50=2.55

      The p-value is the probability that a standard normal distribution exceeds 2.55 in magnitude which is twice the tail probability to the right of 2.55. From tables that tail probability is 1−0.9946=0.0054 and so the p-value is 2×0.0054=0.0108

    2. (b)

      The p-value is small, which provides evidence to reject H0, i.e. it suggests that the population mean is not 120 bushels per acre this year.

    3. (c)

      The answer does not depend on any particular shape, because the sample size is large and so the central limit theorem determines the distribution of the sample average.

  7. 30.

    [Exam standard] True, or false, or depends on context? You must explain your answer to receive marks.

    1. (a)

      We did an experiment where we measured many variables on a random sample of individuals. A careful exploration of the data indicated many interesting, possibly significant, findings. We then carried out various hypothesis tests on the data to check these findings. The conclusions that we draw from these tests are valid.

    2. (b)

      We’ve measured the income of a large random sample of individuals. We’ve drawn a Normal quantile plot to assess the Normality of the data, and we’ve discovered that the distribution is very skewed to the right. This means that we can’t use the Normal distribution in making tests about the population mean μ using the sample mean.

    3. (c)

      We’ve measured the income of a small random sample of individuals. We’ve drawn a Normal quantile plot to assess the Normality of the data, and we’ve discovered that the distribution is very skewed to the right. We don’t know the population variance σ. Ordinarily we could estimate σ by the sample standard deviation s and use the t distribution to make tests about the population mean μ using the sample mean, but the non-Normality of the distribution forbids the use of the t distribution in this case.

    4. (d)

      We’ve calculated a 95% confidence interval for a population mean, μ. The interval is [12.1, 13.4]. This means that P⁢(12.1≤μ≤13.4)=0.95.

    5. (e)

      We’ve carried out an experiment independently 200 times. In each experiment we tested the same null hypothesis at the 1% level of significance. If the null hypothesis is actually true, we should find ourselves mistakenly rejecting the null hypothesis in about two of the experiments.

    6. (f)

      We’ve carried out an experiment and tested a null hypothesis at the 1% level of significance. The probability of a type II error is 0.01.

    7. (g)

      For a two-sided hypothesis test at the 10% level of significance, we could construct a 90% confidence interval, and reject the null hypothesis if the interval does not contain the parameter.

    8. (h)

      For a two-sided hypothesis test at the 10% level of significance, we could construct a 95% confidence interval, and fail to reject the null hypothesis if the interval does not contain the parameter.

    9. (i)

      We’ve independently repeated an experiment 200 times, and tested the same null hypothesis at the 5% level of significance. If the null hypothesis is true, the total number (out of 200) of type I errors is a random variable with a binomial distribution with parameters n=200 and p=0.05. Thus we expect about 10 type I errors, with a standard deviation of about 3.08.

    Solution

    1. (a)

      False. There is nothing to stop you carrying out such tests, and they will be numerically valid, but statistically dubious. Large data sets always contain some unusual patterns, and a number of spurious “significant differences” will arise by chance alone. In general, it is not legitimate to test a hypothesis on the same data that first suggested the hypothesis; instead you should design a second experiment explicitly to test the hypothesis. This does mean collecting more data.

    2. (b)

      False. For large n, the central limit theorem states that the sample mean tends approximately to be Normal whatever the original distribution. We can use the sample mean to make inferences about μ even if we have to estimate the population standard deviation σ by the sample standard deviation s, as the estimate should be quite good for large n.

    3. (c)

      True, although it does depend on the degree of skewness and the size of n.

    4. (d)

      False. A confidence interval is not the same as a probability statement. Instead, in a large number of repeated independent experiments where we calculate 95% confidence intervals, about 95% of the intervals we calculate will contain μ. The confidence refers to the method, not the parameter.

    5. (e)

      True.

    6. (f)

      False. The probability of a type I error is 0.01. The probability of a type II error is not known for this example.

    7. (g)

      True.

    8. (h)

      False in two places. For a two-sided test, if the confidence interval is at 95% the corresponding significance level will be at 5%, not 10%. Secondly, we fail to reject the null hypothesis when the hypothetical value is inside, not outside, the confidence interval.

    9. (i)

      True.

  8. 31.

    You are engaged in designing a clinical trial for testing for side effects of a new drug aimed at ameliorating nausea in pregnant women; for example the drug might or might not be harmful to the unborn child.

    1. (a)

      What are the two hypotheses in this case?

    2. (b)

      What kinds of error might you make?

    3. (c)

      Which kind of error would you try to minimise, and why? Consider a change to the circumstances that could lead you to changing your answer.

    Solution

    1. (a)

      The two hypotheses are as follows. (Some experts would argue that the hypothesis that there are side effects should be the null hypothesis, as the probability of a type I error is well-defined.)

      H0:

      There are no side effects.

      Ha:

      There are side effects.

    2. (b)

      A type I error occurs when H0 is true, but we reject it. That is, we found a significant result indicating side effects even though there are no side effects. A type II error occurs when H0 is false, but we fail to reject it. This corresponds to not finding side effects when there really are side effects.

    3. (c)

      In this example, a type II error is much more serious than a type I error, as it could lead to the marketing of an unsafe drug, compared to a loss of potential profits in the case of a type I error. Hence, we should aim at minimising the type II error. (This would involve using work outside the scope of the course.) A change of circumstances could change our position. If, instead, the drug is aimed at preventing a kind of miscarriage that leads to the certain death of the unborn child, the ethical position becomes much more unclear.

  9. 32.

    The p-value, as used in several of the previous questions to decide whether to reject the null hypothesis H0, is defined in these cases as:

    p-value=P( sample mean is at least as extreme as the observed sample mean|H0 is true)

    An alternative probability was suggested in lectures for consideration:

    P⁢(H0⁢ is true|observed sample mean)
    1. (a)

      Discuss which of these two probabilities seems best suited for making decisions about whether H0 is true.

    2. (b)

      Use Bayes theorem to rewrite P⁢(H0⁢ is true|observed sample mean) in a more useful form, involving “inverted” terms such as P⁢(observed sample mean|H0⁢ is true). Note that you can just use probabilities here, and ignore the subtleties due to continuous random variables for now.

    3. (c)

      Examine the numerator of your answer to part (b). What additional term, that we have not utilised in the entire Frequentist approach up to this point, does Bayes theorem suggest we must inevitably consider if we do indeed want to find P⁢(H0⁢ is true|observed sample mean)? Is this surprising or could it be considered natural?

    4. (d)

      Say there is an alternative hypothesis Ha and that we are sure that either H0 or Ha is true. Can you use the partition theorem to rewrite the denominator of your answer to part (b) using terms that feature either H0 or Ha?

    5. (e)

      We see that the denominator now depends on the form of the alternative hypothesis, and that therefore P⁢(H0⁢ is true|observed sample mean) depends directly on Ha. Comment on whether this is a desirable feature or not.

    6. (f)

      Write down a similar form for P⁢(Ha⁢ is true|observed sample mean). At least up to the level of detail we have used here, is there any major difference between how H0 and Ha are treated in this second (Bayesian) framework? Again, does this seem natural/desirable?

    Solution

    1. (a)

      The p-value is of course informative (and hence why it is so widely used), as an extremely low p-value greatly undermines our belief in H0 being true as the sample mean has landed in such an extreme location, given H0. However, for just small p-values (like around the 5% or 1% level) things are far less clear: here the p-values seem to suggest mild evidence against the null hypothesis H0, but how strong is this exactly? Should we really reject H0? And what about the alternative hypothesis Ha: shouldn’t this feature in our decision too somehow? The problem is that although the p-value is informative regarding H0, it doesn’t tell us exactly what we want for making a decision, which is the actual probability that H0 is true, given the sample data. The second probability provided P⁢(H0⁢ is true|observed sample mean) would provide this if we can calculate it, but note it assumes the sample mean is sufficient (more on this later) for the full sample data.

    2. (b)

      As suggested we ignore issues to do with continuous random variables for now, essentially assuming everything is discrete (we will do these formalities in lectures), and hence can use Bayes theorem to write:

      P⁢(H0⁢ is true|observed sample mean)=P⁢(observed sample mean|H0⁢ is true)⁢P⁢(H0⁢ is true)P⁢(observed sample mean)
    3. (c)

      The numerator of Bayes Theorem suggests we will inevitably have to think about the prior probability of H0, that is our probability before we have seen the data. In other words, Bayes theorem basically says that “if you want (posterior) probabilities of H0 out, then you have to put (prior) probabilities of H0 in”. Whether this is surprising or natural is up to you (but some justification would be nice!).

    4. (d)

      As we are sure that either H0 or Ha is true, we can use the partition theorem as usual and hence have that

      P⁢(H0⁢ is true|observed sample mean)=
      P⁢(observed sample mean|H0⁢ is true)⁢P⁢(H0⁢ is true)P⁢(observed sample mean|H0⁢ is true)⁢P⁢(H0⁢ is true)+P⁢(observed sample mean|Ha⁢ is true)⁢P⁢(Ha⁢ is true)
    5. (e)

      The fact that P⁢(H0⁢ is true|observed sample mean) depends directly on Ha is surely a desirable feature, as surely our decision to reject H0 in favour of Ha should depend in part on the attributes of Ha.

    6. (f)

      Regarding the alternative hypothesis Ha, we have similarly that

      P⁢(Ha⁢ is true|observed sample mean)=
      P⁢(observed sample mean|Ha⁢ is true)⁢P⁢(Ha⁢ is true)P⁢(observed sample mean|H0⁢ is true)⁢P⁢(H0⁢ is true)+P⁢(observed sample mean|Ha⁢ is true)⁢P⁢(Ha⁢ is true)

      Both H0 and Ha are treated in the same way. Indeed if we swapped their order we would still obtain the same posterior probabilities for each. This seems more natural, as the typical elevation of the null hypothesis into something ‘special’ in the standard Frequentist framework does seem a little odd. (In the Frequentist’s defence, there are of course more sophisticated ways of doing hypothesis testing in that framework.)

Hypothesis Testing for Proportions

  1. 33.

    A poll of 1785 US adults asked whether people had attended a place of worship during the last week. 750 respondents said that they had. Pretend that the 1785 people asked form a simple random sample of US adults, and so can be taken to be representative of US adults. (Note: most opinion polls are not simple random samples, and this was no exception.)

    1. (a)

      Give a standard 99% confidence interval for p, the proportion of US adults attending a place of worship during the previous week.

    2. (b)

      Is it fair to conclude that about half of all US adults attended a place of worship during the previous week?

    3. (c)

      How large a sample would be required to obtain a margin of error of ±0.01 in a 99% confidence interval for p, (i) at worst, when p is unknown; (ii) using the observed proportion as a guess for p?

    Solution   Let X be the random variable representing number of attenders at a place of worship. Under the assumption of a simple random sample of people, and assuming that p is the underlying true proportion of attenders in the US population, X has a binomial distribution with parameters n=1785 known and p unknown.

    1. (a)

      The usual estimate of p is y=x/n, where x=750 is the observed number of attenders in this sample. Hence y=750/1785=0.4202 approximately. The standard deviation of Y is p⁢(1−p)n. This is usually estimated, giving the standard error (SE) of Y, by S⁢E⁢(Y)=y⁢(1−y)n=0.0117. For large n, confidence intervals for p can be based on the Normal distribution: A 99% confidence interval is given by

      y±(2.575)⁢y⁢(1−y)n=0.4202±(2.575)⁢(0.0117)=0.4202±0.0301=[0.3901,0.4503].

      Note that the Wilson interval gives the interval [0.3905,0.4505], almost identical to the usual interval. This is inevitable for large sample sizes.

    2. (b)

      Test

      H0:p=0.5
      Ha:p≠0.5

      The 99% confidence interval does not contain the hypothetical value μ=0.5, and so the hypothesis that about half of US adults attended a place of worship the previous week is rejected, at the 1% level of significance.

    3. (c)

      The margin of error for a 99% confidence interval is theoretically ±(2.575)⁢p⁢(1−p)n. This is largest when p=0.5, giving a margin of error of ±(2.575)⁢1/(4⁢n). Simple calculations show that (2.575)⁢1/(4⁢n)≤0.01⇒n≥16576.6, or n=16577. If instead we replace p by y=0.4202 in this calculation, we require (2.575)⁢(0.4202)⁢(0.5798)n≤0.01⇒n≥16154.3, or n=16155.

  2. 34.

    Studies are performed to estimate the percentage of the nation’s asthmatics who are allergic to sulphites. Suppose that 500 asthmatics are randomly selected and that 38 of the 500 are found to be allergic to sulphites.

    1. (a)

      Estimate p, the proportion of all asthmatics who are allergic to sulphites.

    2. (b)

      Find a standard 90% confidence interval for the proportion of all asthmatics who are allergic to sulphites.

    3. (c)

      Test approximately the hypothesis that p=0.08.

    4. (d)

      In the worst possible case, express the variance of the sample proportion as a function of the sample size n. In this worst case, for what value of n do we obtain the 95% confidence interval for p as y±0.01?

      [Hint: for what value of p is the theoretical variance of Y largest? Notice that this part of the question is about the theoretical sampling distribution of Y, and not about the sample we actually obtained.]

    Solution

    1. (a)

      We estimate p by the sample proportion, y=38500=0.076.

    2. (b)

      A confidence interval for p is given by

      y±z⋆⁢y⁢(1−y)n

      with z⋆=1.645 for 90% confidence, as this value gives 5% in each tail of the N(0,1) distribution. Hence we calculate the confidence interval as

      0.076±1.645⁢0.076×0.924500=0.076±1.645×0.0119=0.076±0.020=(0.056,0.096).

      The Wilson interval in this case gives (0.059,0.098). The large sample size implies that the two CIs are close.

    3. (c)
      H0:

      p=0.08.

      Ha:

      p≠0.08.

      The hypothetical value p=0.08 is included in the 90% confidence interval for p, and so we fail to reject the null hypothesis at the 10% level of significance. [NB For proportions, the confidence interval method of hypothesis testing is approximate.]

    4. (d)

      Var⁢[Y]=p⁢(1−p)n≤14⁢n, as the worst possible case occurs when p=12. In this case, at worst the 95% confidence interval for p will be

      y±z∗⁢14⁢n=y±(1.96)⁢14⁢n.

      Thus, we need (1.96)⁢14⁢n=0.01, i.e. n=9604.

  3. 35.

    A supplier of components to the motor industry makes a particular product which sometimes fails immediately it is used. The manufacturing process is controlled so the the proportion of faulty products is supposed to be only 4%. Out of 500 supplied in one batch, 28 prove to be faulty. Has the process gone out of control to produce too many faulty products?

    Solution   Since the suspect there to be too many faulty products, we wish to conduct a 1-sided hypothesis test, with hypotheses:

    H0:

    p=0.04.

    Ha:

    p>0.04.

    where p is the rate of production of faulty objects. We assume that the 500 components are independent, each faulty with this same probability p (binomial model). The Normal approximation is OK since n⁢p0=20 and n⁢(1−p0)=480 are sufficiently large.

    The sample proportion is y=28/500=0.056. 80% and 90% confidence intervals for p are given respectively by

    0.056±1.282⁢0.056×0.944500=0.056±1.282×0.0103=0.056±0.013=[0.043,0.069].
    0.056±1.645⁢0.056×0.944500=0.056±1.645×0.0103=0.056±0.017=[0.039,0.073].

    The hypothetical value of p,p=0.04, falls outside the lower end of the 80% confidence interval, and so there is evidence to reject the null hypothesis at the 10% level (for a one-sided test). However, p = 0.04 falls just inside the lower end of the 90% confidence interval, and so we would fail to reject the null hypothesis at the 5% level (for a one-sided test). Something unusual has occurred, but not something very unusual.
